conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been feeling really nauseous since this morning and I’ve thrown up a few times. It’s been hard to keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You have a history of gastroparesis, right? That’s when the stomach doesn’t empty properly, often due to diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. I have Type 1 diabetes and my stomach has always been slow. I have a gastric pacemaker to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right, and we checked — your pacemaker looks intact on the X-ray. No changes. We also did a chest X-ray because we saw something unclear in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh? Is something wrong with my lungs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not likely. There was a faint shadow near your shoulder blade, but it might just be how you were positioned. A repeat X-ray showed clear lungs. So we think it’s nothing serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried it might be pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We also checked your heart enzymes because your initial ones were a bit high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Heart enzymes? Do I have heart damage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not at all. Your first CK-MB was elevated, but we repeated the test — it’s now normal. Troponin, which is more specific for heart injury, was always negative. So it’s likely a lab anomaly, not a heart issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. I don’t have chest pain or anything, so that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Right now, your main issue is the gastroparesis flare. We’re giving you IV fluids and anti-nausea meds like Zofran and Compazine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already feel a little better since the shot in the ER. But why did this happen now? I didn’t change my diet or insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes these flares happen without a clear trigger. Stress, blood sugar swings, or even just the chronic nerve damage from diabetes can cause it. Your blood sugar was 238 in the ER — a bit high, but not extreme.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, my sugars have been running in the 200s lately, even though I’m not eating much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common with gastroparesis. We’ve been giving you insulin on a sliding scale here, and your sugars have been much better — in the 100s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So should I adjust my insulin at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep your insulin the same for now. But we are starting you on two new medications: a baby aspirin daily and a low-dose lisinopril.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why aspirin and lisinopril? I don’t have heart or kidney problems.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With long-term Type 1 diabetes, we use these to prevent complications. Aspirin helps protect your heart, and lisinopril protects your kidneys, especially if there’s early signs of damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. That makes sense. I didn’t know I needed that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Just checking in. How’s the nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I haven’t vomited since I got here. Still feel a little queasy, but not as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re going to try advancing your diet — start with clear liquids and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have water or broth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Small sips at first. We’ll watch you closely. If you keep it down, we’ll move to soft foods tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You made it through the night without vomiting. You’re on a soft diet now — how are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I had some applesauce and toast this morning and it stayed down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent progress. We’ll keep the IV fluids running for now but plan to switch you back to oral meds soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re aiming for discharge in a couple of days. We want to make sure you’re tolerating a regular diet and your blood sugars stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. You’re doing well. You’ve had a regular meal and kept it down. Your blood sugar is 112 — perfect.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel almost back to normal. Can I stop the IV now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll remove the IV today. You’ll go back to your regular insulin — glargine at night and lispro as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the new pills — aspirin and lisinopril — I take those every day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. One baby aspirin daily, and half a lisinopril tablet once a day. We’ll increase it slowly if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about the nausea meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have lorazepam and Phenergan to take as needed if nausea comes back. But try to avoid overusing them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember the nurse said something about my gastric pacemaker being checked later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, Dr. Patel will check it as an outpatient. It looks fine now, but we want to make sure it’s working optimally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two full days without vomiting and you’re eating normally. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If nausea comes back and you can’t keep fluids down, or if you develop fever, chest pain, or trouble breathing, call your doctor or go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your endocrinologist in a week. And Dr. Patel will schedule the pacemaker check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. You’re stable, tolerating food, and your labs are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: take your new meds daily, monitor your sugars, and call if anything worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been feeling nauseous and vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, since last night. I had dinner like normal, but then I started feeling sick and threw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Did you notice any blood in the vomit?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It looked kind of like coffee grounds. Is that bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That can mean there’s some irritation or bleeding in the stomach or esophagus. Given your history of gastroparesis and diabetes, this isn’t uncommon during a flare-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had anything to eat today. My stomach just feels full and heavy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’re going to start you on IV fluids to rehydrate you and give you some anti-nausea medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Should I still take my insulin even though I’m not eating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. You must never skip your insulin, even if you're not eating. We’ll adjust the doses based on your blood sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I’ve been worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve ordered some blood tests and a chest X-ray to make sure there’s no infection or other issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a chest X-ray before, right? For the last admission?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and this one looks similar—no pneumonia or pneumothorax. Your heart size is normal, and the gastric pacer leads are still in place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very good. We also did an abdominal X-ray. It shows your bowels aren’t blocked, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been admitted a few times for this. Is this just another flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks like a gastroparesis flare, yes. We’re giving you your usual metoclopramide and adding compazine for nausea control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve heard sometimes people make themselves throw up. I don’t do that, just so you know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for saying that. We just need to understand all possibilities. Your labs show mild dehydration and slightly high white blood cells, but no infection so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my blood pressure? It’s usually high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a bit elevated today—167 over 84. We’ll keep an eye on it. Your lisinopril dose may be adjusted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. I didn’t vomit last night, but I still don’t feel like eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’re going to try starting you on small sips of ginger ale and see if you can tolerate toast later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My mouth is still dry, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing IV fluids to help with that. Your blood sugar has been stable, which is helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a urine test last night. Was there anything wrong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It showed mixed bacteria, but that’s likely from contamination. No sign of a urinary infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You kept down toast and applesauce yesterday. We’re going to advance your diet to soft foods today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting there. We want to make sure you can keep food and meds down. We’re also adjusting your medications for long-term protection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like what?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re increasing your lisinopril to 7.5 mg daily to protect your kidneys from diabetes damage. And we’re starting a baby aspirin for heart protection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember starting those last time. Are they working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and it’s important to stay on them. We’re also giving you both oral and rectal compazine in case nausea comes back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The rectal one? I’ve never used that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s helpful if you can’t keep pills down. It works well for nausea and is safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You’ve had two meals without vomiting. That’s great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling more like myself. Can I go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if you continue to do well. We’ll write your discharge orders today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I do if I start feeling sick again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take the compazine as prescribed. Avoid large meals, soda, or eating too fast. And never skip insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if it doesn’t help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or come back if you have fever, chest pain, trouble breathing, or severe pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. You’re stable, eating, and taking your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll follow up with my clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Make sure you take the pantoprazole daily for your esophagitis. It helps reduce stomach acid and irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll start it today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Keep your blood sugar in check—it helps prevent these flares. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check-in before discharge. Any nausea now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel okay. A bit tired, but no nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Remember—small, frequent meals. No skipping insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And take the new meds every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re all set. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—we reviewed your labs and imaging. Everything supports a gastroparesis flare with no complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the coffee ground vomit wasn’t serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It suggests mild bleeding, likely from esophagitis or a small tear from vomiting. The pantoprazole will help heal that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your discharge instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I think I’ve got it all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad you’re feeling better. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check—any questions before you go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m good. All set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you’ve been having nausea and vomiting again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, since yesterday morning. I’ve thrown up over ten times—greenish stuff, not bloody. I couldn’t keep anything down except a little ginger ale in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds really tough. Any pain, fever, or diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No pain or fever, but I feel chills and so tired. It’s like my usual gastroparesis flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Your vitals show you’re a bit tachycardic and your blood pressure was high earlier, but it’s come down. We’ll start IV fluids and some anti-nausea meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I took a compazine suppository at home—it helped a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. We gave you IV compazine, Zofran, and fluids in the ER. You also got insulin since your blood sugar was high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How’s my blood sugar now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s stable. We adjusted your insulin while you’re not eating. You’ll continue your usual Lantus at night and resume your sliding scale when you can eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. I’ve had three admissions this month—worried something’s wrong with my gastric pacer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you had it checked recently. Since then, you’ve had two more flares. Dr. Patel said unless things worsen, we’ll keep your current plan. But you can stop by his clinic any afternoon if you’re concerned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. What about my blood pressure? It’s been all over the place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been labile. You were on clonidine before but stopped. We’re restarting a clonidine patch—once a week. It’s better for you since you vomit so often.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forgot to pick up the prescription last time. Will I get it this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re sending it to your pharmacy. But you’ll need to follow up with your PCP to keep it going. We’re also adjusting your lisinopril to 7.5 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. My white blood cell count was high—should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was 15.8, but no fever or infection signs. Likely from dehydration and stress. It’s already down to 7.0 today—back to normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my stomach? Any blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray—no obstruction or free air. Lungs are clear. Your gastric pacer leads are in place. So no signs of perforation or blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been on Reglan at home—will I keep that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re giving IV Reglan every six hours. Once you can eat, we’ll switch back to oral—same dose, four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I haven’t vomited since last night. I sipped some broth—kept it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’ll try advancing your diet to soft foods today—like toast and applesauce. Small amounts, slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have ginger ale? Regular, not diet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, regular ginger ale is fine. In fact, if you’re only tolerating clear liquids at home, it’s better to have regular ones to avoid ketosis, especially with your diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know that. I’ve been sticking to diet drinks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With your history, if you’re not eating enough, your body can go into ketosis. So regular clear liquids are okay short-term. But resume your diabetic diet when you can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well today—kept down soup, crackers, and juice. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if this continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What meds will I go home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before: Protonix for GERD, Reglan four times a day, aspirin, and your insulin. Plus, we’re adding the clonidine patch for blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And lisinopril?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, now 7.5 mg daily. But we’re writing it as 5 mg tablets—you’ll take one and a half each day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have an appointment with Dr. Patel in two weeks for your pacer. If symptoms worsen before then, you can walk in to his clinic any afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I start vomiting again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Go back to clear liquids. If you can only keep those down, it’s okay to have regular ones to prevent ketosis. But if you develop fever, chest pain, or trouble breathing, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had no vomiting overnight and ate a light breakfast. We’re clearing you for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Just to confirm—I’m taking the clonidine patch weekly, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one patch weekly. And keep all your other meds. Follow up with your PCP about the patch and your blood pressure control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel chills or fatigue again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Monitor your symptoms. Fatigue and chills can be part of a flare. But if you spike a fever or feel worse, call your doctor or return here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers and prescriptions ready. You should be out by 10 a.m.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—my urine test showed ketones earlier, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s why we emphasized regular clear liquids. It helps prevent your body from breaking down fat for energy when you’re not eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ll watch that at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re doing great. Just take it slow with food and keep up with your follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in clinic if needed, but hopefully not in the hospital again soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. I’ve also been feeling really dizzy and my heart’s racing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s probably from dehydration. Your heart rate was elevated when you arrived. We’re giving you IV fluids to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that makes sense. I haven’t had anything to drink all day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve also started you on anti-nausea medications—Zofran, Compazine, and Ativan—to help settle your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve taken Compazine at home before. It helps a little, but not completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I’m glad to hear that. I’ve had high readings at home lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No pain, just the nausea and vomiting. I’m just so tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common with dehydration and poor intake. The fluids should help you feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you today. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’ve been having really bad nausea and vomiting all morning. It’s like my usual gastroparesis flare, but worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no pain or fever. But I did throw up a little blood when I got here. That scared me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. We’ll keep an eye on that. You also mentioned chills—any other new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just the chills since I’ve been here. Otherwise, same as usual—just can’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We gave you Zofran and Ativan in the ER for nausea. After the Ativan, your breathing slowed and oxygen dropped, so we moved you to ICU for monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Wait—was that because of the Ativan? I’ve taken it before without problems.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was likely the 1 mg IV dose. You usually take 0.25 mg by mouth, right? Higher IV doses can affect breathing, especially if you're already unwell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So I should avoid higher doses then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll make a note in your chart. You’re breathing fine now, which is great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs came back. Blood sugar was high—302 this morning. We’re watching for signs of DKA, but you’re not in it. We adjusted your insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My sugars have been running high lately. Did we figure out why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely due to vomiting—you can’t keep food or meds down, so insulin balance gets thrown off. We’re giving you IV fluids and adjusting your coverage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about the blood I vomited?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s from a small tear in the esophagus—called a Mallory-Weiss tear—caused by forceful vomiting. Your hemoglobin is stable, so no active bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. We’ve stopped your aspirin temporarily and started a stronger stomach protector—Protonix twice daily for six weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood pressure spiked last night—up to 215/140. That’s called hypertensive urgency. We gave IV meds to bring it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was that because of the vomiting or stress?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely both, and you couldn’t take your lisinopril by mouth. We restarted it today now that you’re tolerating liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Are my sugars better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ve come down with adjusted insulin. We’ll keep monitoring and get you back to your home regimen before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve added IV erythromycin. It helps with stomach emptying and might be useful for your gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve never taken that before. Is it safe with my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve checked. It’s a short course. We’ll stop it when you leave, but you should discuss continuing it with your GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing better. You’ve kept down clear liquids and your nausea is less. We’re going to try small amounts of soft food today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I’m hungry, but I’m nervous about vomiting again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. We’ll go slow—small bites, frequent checks. If you keep it down, we’ll advance further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great job—you tolerated applesauce and crackers. We’re upgrading to a soft diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my gastric pacer? It hasn’t been helping as much lately.

conversation_lines.text: Good point. Dr. ___ is back next week. We’ll schedule a pacer check to see if it needs adjustment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure is still a bit high, but more stable. We used hydralazine for peaks, but now it’s mostly controlled with your usual meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. That helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: Good to know. Any other tests?

conversation_lines.text: We did a MRSA screen—negative, so no infection concern. Main issues remain gastroparesis, blood pressure, and blood sugar control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. You’re on a regular diet, no vomiting, and labs are stable. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! What meds will I go home on?

conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the erythromycin?

conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. You’re stable, eating well, and symptoms are controlled.

conversation_lines.text: Thank you. Any warning signs I should watch for?

conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. And keep using your anti-nausea meds early. We’re discharging you in stable condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad this round wasn’t as bad as the last one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We caught it early, adjusted your pacer, and treated the esophagitis. That should help prevent frequent admissions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope so. Ten times in three months is too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re working on it. Take care, and call if anything concerns you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your prescriptions and discharge instructions now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait for her.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing much better. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you’ve been feeling very nauseous and vomiting since this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I woke up feeling awful. I’ve thrown up greenish fluid several times. I tried to take my pills but I just vomited them right back up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned you’ve had this happen before—about 10 times in the last three months?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. But after my last hospital stay, my GI doctor adjusted my gastric pacer and gave me new meds. I was fine for a full week—then this hit again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s frustrating. Your vitals show high blood pressure and a fast heart rate, which we often see during these episodes. We’ll start IV fluids and give you some anti-nausea meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that be enough? Last time, nothing helped until they adjusted the pacer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you Zofran, Reglan, and Compazine now. But we’ll also check if there’s another issue. An abdominal X-ray was done—no blockage, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My blood sugar was high earlier—should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your fingerstick glucose was 349. Since you’re not eating, we’ve started a lower dose of Lantus insulin and will use Humalog as needed. We’ll monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from last night were stable—no infection in blood cultures, kidney function is normal. But your heart rate is still in the 110s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel anxious, but I know it’s from being so sick. Is the fast heart rate dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely a stress response to nausea and vomiting. It usually improves when symptoms do. We’re watching it on telemetry, and your ECG shows just sinus tachycardia—no heart damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re considering an endoscopy. Since you’ve had esophagitis before, we want to check if that’s flaring up or if the pylorus is too tight, slowing stomach emptying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had that last time. They found esophagitis and adjusted my pacer. Could we do something more this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. If the pylorus is tight, we can inject Botox to relax it. It’s been helpful for some patients with gastroparesis like yours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds worth trying. When would it happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve scheduled it for tomorrow morning. For now, we’ll keep you on IV fluids and continue the anti-nausea meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure is still high—188/88. We gave hydralazine yesterday, but it’s not fully controlled. We’ll restart your lisinopril once you can keep pills down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on lisinopril for years. Should I be concerned it’s not working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely because you haven’t been able to take it. Once we restart it and your nausea improves, we expect your BP to come down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. Any update on the endoscopy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still on for today. We’ll also repeat your chest X-ray to check your port and lungs. You had a portable one last night—heart size is normal, lungs are clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re about to take you for your endoscopy. You’ll be sedated, and the GI team will look at your esophagus and stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And they’ll do the Botox if needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if they see the pylorus is tight. We’ll update you when you wake up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The endoscopy went well. You had some inflammation and a small ulcer at the bottom of your esophagus—consistent with reflux. The stomach was empty, which confirms delayed emptying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Botox?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they injected Botox into the pylorus to help it relax. This should help food move from your stomach into the intestine more easily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Do I need to stay on the same meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on Protonix twice daily for the esophagitis, and continue Reglan and erythromycin to help stomach motility. Your nausea should start improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you made it through the night without vomiting. We’re going to try advancing your diet to clear liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m actually feeling less nauseous. Could the Botox be working already?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. It can take a few days, but some patients feel better quickly. We’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My heart rate is still high—118. Should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s still elevated, but it’s coming down slowly. As your nausea improves, we expect your heart rate and blood pressure to normalize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated clear liquids well. We’re going to try a soft diabetic diet—mashed potatoes, applesauce, things like that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m hungry for real food. Can I have insulin with it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll restart your full insulin regimen—Lantus at night and Humalog before meals. Your glucose was 153 this morning—well controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Any other labs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your potassium was low yesterday—2.9—so we gave supplements. This morning it’s 3.4, which is better but still a bit low. We’ll keep giving potassium with your meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t realize that could happen. Is it from vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Losing fluids through vomiting can deplete potassium. We’re replacing it, so it should normalize soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two meals and no vomiting. Your heart rate is down to 98, and BP is 138/82. We think you’re ready to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. Are my meds the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—same doses. Continue Protonix twice daily, Reglan four times a day, erythromycin three times a day, and your insulin. Use Zofran or the suppository if nausea returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your GI doctor in one week to check how you’re doing with the Botox. Also follow up with your endocrinologist for diabetes management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I start vomiting again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or come back if you can’t keep food or liquids down, or if you have chest pain, high fever, or vomit blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for getting me through this episode.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. The Botox may help reduce how often this happens. We’ll keep working to get you more stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I really hope so. Ten admissions in three months is too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re all on your side. Let’s aim for fewer trips back. Your husband can pick you up around noon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: He’ll be relieved. Thanks again, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed, but I hope not!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in—how are you feeling after breakfast?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still no nausea. I ate most of my oatmeal and drank tea. I think I’m really turning a corner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’ll finalize your discharge paperwork soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so grateful. This episode was scary, but I feel much better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad too. Keep up with your diet, meds, and follow-up. You’ve made great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will come by to review your medications and discharge instructions one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ve got my list. I’ll take everything as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your discharge labs show mild anemia and low potassium, but both are improving. No need for transfusion or extra treatment now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I take iron or anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not unless your outpatient doctor recommends it. Focus on nutrition and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with my kidneys? I’ve had kidney issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, good to know. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back negative—no infection in the blood. Urine culture was contaminated, so not reliable.

conversation_lines.text: So no UTI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from the endoscopy. You did great. We found white patches in your esophagus—signs of a fungal infection called candidiasis.

conversation_lines.text: A fungal infection? But I feel fine otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How do we treat it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Did you do the Botox injection too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope it works again. What about the inflammation you mentioned last time?

conversation_lines.text: I was on something for that before. This is stronger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, twice daily should help reduce irritation and possibly the nausea too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you kept down some apple juice and crackers last night. That’s a big step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was so nervous, but it stayed down. Can I eat more today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll advance you to a soft diet—things like mashed potatoes, oatmeal. Small, frequent meals are best with gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin? I took my glargine last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we restarted your glargine. Your fasting sugar this morning was 144—excellent. Keep using your humalog as needed with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. My blood pressure has been better too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, on lisinopril, it’s been in the 140s over 80s. Much improved. We’ll keep you on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two full meals and no vomiting. We think you’re ready to go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s wonderful. What meds am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: And Zofran for nausea if it comes back?

conversation_lines.text: Yes, there’s a small area of pneumonia in your left lower lung. Given your vomiting, it’s likely you aspirated—bacteria got into your lungs when you threw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t even feel sick with a cold or anything. Can we treat it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re starting antibiotics—levofloxacin and metronidazole—for about a week. Blood cultures were negative, so no bloodstream infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. Will the antibiotics make me feel worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some people get mild stomach upset, but we’ll monitor. Your main issue is still the gastroparesis flare. We’ve consulted GI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The GI team recommends an EGD with Botox injection into your stomach. It can help relax the muscles and improve emptying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve heard of that. Is it safe? Will it help quickly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s low risk and often helps within a few days. You’ll be sedated, and it takes about 30 minutes. We’ll schedule it for tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do it. I just want to stop vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also adjusting your insulin. Your sugars have been high—over 300—likely from stress and vomiting. We’re increasing your Lantus to 30 units at bedtime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my diabetes getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. This is likely temporary. Once your stomach settles, your sugars should stabilize. But we’ll follow up with your endocrinologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from the EGD. You tolerated it well. They injected Botox into your pylorus. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still a bit groggy, but no nausea yet. That’s a first in days!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll start you on clear liquids and see how you do. The Botox should help over the next few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat real food soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll advance slowly. If you keep the liquids down, we’ll try soft foods tomorrow. Also, your blood pressure was high on admission, but it’s better now. We switched you back to your oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was that from the vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely due to stress and dehydration. It’s improving with treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just drank some apple juice and felt okay. No urge to vomit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent progress. We’ll order a soft diet for dinner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pneumonia? Is it getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The antibiotics are working. You’re not running a fever, and your cough is mild. Continue the levofloxacin and Flagyl for four more days after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any other follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. GI wants you to have a colonoscopy as an outpatient. Also, follow up with your endocrinologist about your insulin adjustment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I have that appointment next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve made great progress. No vomiting, eating soft foods, and your lungs are clearing. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news! What meds will I go home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before, but with two new antibiotics: levofloxacin once daily and metronidazole three times a day for four days. We also increased your Lantus to 30 units at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the nausea meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can still use ondansetron or prochlorperazine as needed. The scopolamine patch and domperidone continue as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I watch for any warning signs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. If nausea returns, or you develop fever, shortness of breath, or chest pain, come back right away. Otherwise, keep your follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. The Botox should help for several months. We’ll see how you do and adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m hopeful. I really appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You should be able to go home in a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my iron levels. I think I’ve been low before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noted iron deficiency anemia. It’s not severe, but your PCP can check it with a blood test in a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll follow up on that too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. How’s your energy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I’m still tired, but not nauseated at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Keep resting and taking your meds. You’re cleared to go home soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. You’re in the ICU because your blood sugar was very high and you’re in diabetic ketoacidosis. We’ve started you on fluids and insulin through an IV to help correct that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I’ve been here before for this. I took my Lantus this morning and used my sliding scale, but I just couldn’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your glucose was 637 when you arrived, and your anion gap was elevated, which confirms DKA. We’re giving you an insulin drip now to bring that down safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been nauseous all day. Started vomiting around 7 p.m. I didn’t eat much. Is that why this happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely a big part of it. Poor intake and vomiting can throw off your insulin balance. We’re also treating your nausea with Zofran and Compazine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still feeling shaky and my heart’s racing. Is that from the DKA?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the high blood sugar and dehydration can cause tachycardia—your heart rate is 129. We’re watching it closely. It should improve as we correct your fluids and sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also saw some peaked T-waves on your EKG, and your potassium was high at 5.6. We’re monitoring that carefully to prevent any heart rhythm issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s scary. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We caught it early. Your levels are coming down with treatment. No signs of a heart attack—we checked your enzymes and they were normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had so many DKA episodes because of my gastroparesis. The Botox didn’t help much last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you had an EGD with Botox recently. Unfortunately, it sounds like it hasn’t provided lasting relief. We’re focusing on symptom control for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I noticed some dark flecks in my vomit. Is that blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Given your history of esophagitis, it could be from irritation in your esophagus. We’ve started you on an IV proton pump inhibitor to protect your stomach lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried about bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is stable. The dark flecks are likely old blood. We’ll keep an eye on it, but you’re not showing signs of active bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from a few hours ago show your glucose is down to 217 and your anion gap is closing. That’s a great sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel a little less shaky. Can I eat something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We want to make sure your nausea is under control and your sugars stay stable. We’ll try small sips later if you’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been off my blood pressure meds—metoprolol and lisinopril. Should I restart them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held them initially because your blood pressure and heart rate were high from DKA. Once you’re more stable, we’ll restart them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your urine test back. There was a possible E. coli, so we started you on cipro just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t have any burning when I pee. Could it be a false alarm?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. The lab noted contamination from skin flora, so it might not be a real infection. We’ll repeat the test and stop antibiotics if it’s negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The repeat urine culture showed contamination again. No true UTI. We’re stopping the cipro.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great, I didn’t want to take more antibiotics. I’m still on metronidazole—should I stop that too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were supposed to finish that course a few days ago. Since you’re still taking it, we’ll have you stop now to avoid unnecessary side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your anion gap is now normal, and your blood sugars are between 150 and 200. We’re switching you from the insulin drip to subcutaneous insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll go back to my Lantus and Humalog?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll get 30 units of Lantus at bedtime and use Humalog as a sliding scale four times a day. We’ll monitor your levels closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s what I was on before. I hope it keeps me stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray today. No signs of pneumonia. Your lungs look clear, which is good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had pneumonia last time I was here. I was worried it came back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, your lungs are clear. The previous opacity has resolved. This time, your DKA was triggered by gastroparesis, not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated a small meal earlier without vomiting. That’s a big improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I actually felt hungry. Can I eat more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll advance your diet slowly—soft foods first. Your nausea has improved, so that’s promising.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I hate being on IV fluids. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you keep doing well—eating, stable sugars, no vomiting—we’re looking at discharge tomorrow or the day after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning are excellent. Anion gap closed, no ketones, sugars 100–180. You’ve had two meals without issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my blood pressure meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve restarted your metoprolol and lisinopril. Your blood pressure is now well-controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Nexium? I wasn’t taking it, but I know I should.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching you to pantoprazole 40 mg daily. It’s similar and will help with your esophagitis and those dark flecks in your vomit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing so well. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Monitor your blood sugar closely. If you start vomiting again or can’t keep food down, check for ketones and come in early.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Should I follow up with my endocrinologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, within a week. Also with GI to discuss long-term options for your gastroparesis. The Botox hasn’t helped much, so other treatments may be needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. All set for discharge. You’re on Lantus 30 units at bedtime, Humalog sliding scale, and your other meds as we discussed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No changes, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Continue everything as prescribed. Take the pantoprazole daily, even if you feel fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for helping me get through this again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay hydrated, eat small meals, and don’t hesitate to call or come in if things go off track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be careful. I don’t want to be back here soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do our best to prevent that. Take care, and I’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee. You were brought in because of nausea and vomiting. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… I woke up this morning feeling fine, but then my blood sugar was in the 200s, and I started vomiting. It’s just like my last flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, and you’ve had this before with your gastroparesis. Are you able to keep anything down at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not even water. I threw up once this morning and it’s been nonstop since.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your blood pressure is quite high—210 over 100—and your heart rate is fast, 140. That’s common during these episodes, but we’ll need to manage it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It always goes up when I’m sick. But I stopped my blood pressure meds a few days ago… I thought I didn’t need them anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be part of why it’s so high. We’ll restart those, but for now, we’re giving you fluids and medications through your port to help with the nausea and vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. My stomach just won’t settle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve given you Zofran, Compazine, and Ativan for nausea. Your labs show your blood sugar was high—323—and your bicarbonate is a bit low, which means mild acidosis. But no severe ketoacidosis this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not DKA again? I was so sick last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not full DKA. You have trace ketones, but your anion gap is closing. We’re continuing your long-acting insulin and using a sliding scale for corrections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my liver tests? I saw something about elevated enzymes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your ALT and AST are elevated—69 and 82—higher than usual for you. But they weren’t extremely high, and we don’t think it’s from Tylenol or infection. We’ll check them again at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t taken any Tylenol. Could it be from the Botox injection I had six months ago?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but we don’t have proof. The GI team thinks your symptoms are more related to your gastroparesis flaring up again. They recommend restarting Reglan and continuing pantoprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember Reglan helps. But will I need another Botox injection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The GI team suggested considering it during your outpatient colonoscopy, especially since you have iron deficiency anemia. You’ll discuss that with your gastroenterologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. And my gastric pacer—should the settings be adjusted?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you should follow up with Dr. ___ to evaluate if the neurostimulator settings need changing. That could help reduce these flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing better—no vomiting since last night. You’re on IV fluids and your blood sugars are stabilizing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I feel a bit better. Can I try drinking something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with small sips of water. If you keep that down, we’ll advance to clear liquids and then soft foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. And my blood pressure? It was so high yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave IV metoprolol yesterday, and now we’re restarting your home meds—lisinopril and metoprolol twice daily. Your heart rate is down to 90 today, which is much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to take them regularly from now on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning show your bicarbonate is up to 24, so the acidosis has resolved. Liver enzymes are trending down slightly too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. So I’m improving on all fronts?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ve kept down apple juice and crackers. We’ll move you to a soft diet and plan for discharge tomorrow if this continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. What meds will I go home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue glargine insulin at night and the humalog sliding scale. Also, Reglan with meals, pantoprazole daily, and your blood pressure meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Zofran and Compazine for if I get nauseous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, Zofran ODT as needed every eight hours, and Compazine suppositories up to twice a day. But avoid driving with those—they can make you drowsy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’ve tolerated a full soft meal and no vomiting. We’re clearing you for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. What should I do at home to prevent this from happening again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Eat small, frequent meals and stay upright for at least 30 minutes after eating. Keep up with your Reglan and pantoprazole. And don’t skip your blood pressure meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I need to schedule the colonoscopy and see my GI doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Also follow up with your primary care doctor to review your liver tests and medication plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my husband has my emergency contact info, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we have his number. Call us if you start vomiting again, can’t keep insulin down, or your blood sugar goes very high or low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you so much for helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You did well. We’ll get your discharge papers ready, and you should be home within a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave—still feeling okay? No nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel much better. I even had toast and tea this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Remember to take your meds as prescribed and follow up with your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes. I woke up this morning with sudden nausea and started vomiting—like every 20 or 30 minutes. I’ve been doing this all day. It feels just like my past gastroparesis flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You have Type 1 diabetes and a gastric pacer for gastroparesis, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. I’ve had the pacer for about a year now. I’ve been on Reglan, Pantoprazole, and my insulin. I haven’t missed any doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. You also mentioned loose stools a few times today—is that usual during a flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, sometimes when my stomach’s not moving, things get messy lower down too. But no blood in the stool or anything like that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. Any fevers, chest pain, or black or coffee-ground-like vomit?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing like that. Just constant nausea and vomiting. I couldn’t even keep water down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. In the ER, they gave you IV fluids, Zofran, Compazine, and Ativan. Your blood sugar was high—277—and now it’s 309. We’ll manage that with insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but the Ativan really helped. After that last dose, I felt way better—almost normal. Why is that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s interesting. Ativan can help with nausea, especially if anxiety is making it worse. But the fact that it worked so dramatically makes us wonder if this episode might also be related to benzodiazepine withdrawal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Wait—withdrawal? I haven’t been on any Ativan regularly. I only take it if I’m really anxious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible you’ve used it enough in the past that stopping suddenly could cause symptoms. Or it might just be that it’s very effective for your type of nausea. We’ll keep an eye on that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But I feel so much better now. Can I go home? I have a big meeting tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but you’ve been vomiting nonstop for hours, and you’re still on IV fluids and anti-nausea meds. We need to make sure you can keep food down and that this doesn’t come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I already ate a few crackers an hour ago and didn’t throw up. I feel fine now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. But you were just started on oral intake. We usually like to watch for at least 12–24 hours to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I get that, but I really can’t stay. Is there anything you can give me to take home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can give you oral anti-nausea meds and a few Ativan tablets to help prevent withdrawal symptoms, just in case. But you need to follow up with your PCP within the next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I promise I’ll call them tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, your labs came back. White count is a bit high, but not concerning. Your liver and pancreas enzymes are normal, which is good—rules out other causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood sugar? It’s always high during flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 309 is high, but expected with stress and vomiting. We’re giving insulin to manage it. Keep using your sliding scale at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my other meds? Should I restart Reglan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re sending you home with Reglan, Zofran, Compazine, and your usual meds. Take them as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Ativan? How many should I take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
