conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. Some patients develop dependence even with occasional use. The fact that Ativan stopped your symptoms so quickly raises that possibility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s scary. Should I stop using it completely?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily—but use it sparingly. Discuss it with your PCP. They might suggest tapering or alternatives.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I will. What about my iron? I’ve had anemia for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is 33.9%—low but stable. No sign of active bleeding. Continue your iron supplements if you’re on them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take one daily. Should I take more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not without checking with your doctor. Too much iron can be harmful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. And my blood pressure? It’s always high when I’m stressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was 155/85 when you arrived—elevated but not dangerous. Keep taking your lisinopril and metoprolol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t missed those. They’re part of my morning routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep all your chronic meds the same. The main issue was the nausea episode.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So you’re saying I can go home? I just need to promise to follow up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but you’re signing out against medical advice. That means we’re concerned you might relapse, but we respect your decision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I feel fine now, and I really need to get back. I’ll call my doctor tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright. We’ll get the discharge papers ready. Take it easy, eat small meals, and don’t hesitate to come back if vomiting returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I really appreciate the help. The Ativan was a game-changer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Just use it carefully. We’re sending a summary to your PCP so they’re aware.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Should I mention the possibility of withdrawal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, definitely. They might want to evaluate your benzodiazepine use and consider a slow taper if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. And I’ll keep using my gastric pacer as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s there to help with gastroparesis. If flares keep happening, your team might adjust the settings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll bring that up. Thanks again, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and please follow up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Feel better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. Nurse will be in with your discharge instructions and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I’ll wait here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your vomit tested positive for blood. But given your history of esophagitis, it’s likely from irritation, not serious bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that makes sense. I sometimes get heartburn after vomiting a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Keep taking your Pantoprazole daily to protect your stomach and esophagus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t skip it. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Stay hydrated, eat small meals, and monitor your blood sugar closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I’ll text you if anything comes up—wait, no, I’ll call my PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please do. Or come back to the ER if you can’t keep fluids down again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to go through that again anytime soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do our best to help prevent that. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Nurse is on her way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll wait.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care and feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were brought in this morning for nausea and vomiting. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I woke up at 5 a.m. and started vomiting—six times already. It’s been really bad. I even saw some dark stuff in it, like old coffee grounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. That’s concerning. The ER team mentioned it tested positive for blood, but not bright red. That usually means it’s from the stomach, not fresh bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s scary. Is my stomach bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely from irritation due to all the vomiting—what we call gastritis. Your hematocrit is stable, so no major blood loss. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. My diabetes and gastroparesis have been acting up lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your history of gastroparesis—delayed stomach emptying—can definitely cause this. We’re going to keep you NPO for now, meaning nothing by mouth, to let your stomach rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No food? How long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just for now. We’ll start with IV fluids to keep you hydrated and slowly add back liquids once the vomiting stops.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. My blood sugar must be high then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was 295 this morning. We’ve reduced your long-acting insulin to 18 units since you’re not eating. We’ll increase it as needed and get you back on your regular dose when you start eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also giving you several anti-nausea medications—Reglan, Zofran, Compazine, and Ativan. They work in different ways to help control the vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve taken those before. Ativan helped last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. We’ll keep using it. Also, your blood pressure is elevated—184 over 70. You mentioned you weren’t taking your lisinopril or metoprolol at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I stopped them after my last discharge. I thought they weren’t necessary if I felt okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re important for long-term heart and kidney protection, especially with diabetes. We’ve restarted them since your BP stayed high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take them regularly from now on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also started an IV medication called pantoprazole. It reduces stomach acid and helps the irritated lining heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that for the bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Even a small amount of blood in vomit means we need to protect your stomach. Once you can eat, we’ll switch to the pill form.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Should I be worried about my heart? The EKG showed something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your EKG shows sinus tachycardia—your heart rate is fast, about 105. That’s likely from dehydration and nausea, not a heart problem. Your chest X-ray was normal too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing better—only one episode of vomiting yesterday and none since. We’re going to try clear liquids today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great! I feel less nauseated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your blood sugar is coming down. We increased your Lantus to 23 units yesterday because 18 wasn’t enough. We’ll keep adjusting as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. Can I eat real food soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you tolerate liquids today, we’ll try soft foods tomorrow. We’re also restarting your citalopram—you’ve been off it since admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling anxious. I’m glad to restart it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also continuing the heparin injections to prevent blood clots, since you’re not moving around much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning! You made it through clear liquids and soft foods with no vomiting. That’s excellent progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better. Can I go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re on track for discharge tomorrow. We want to make sure you can keep food down and your blood sugar stays stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. What about my gastric pacer? Could that be part of the problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. Your GI doctor has been notified, and you’re scheduled to follow up with them. They may consider adjusting the settings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had botox in my stomach before too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s an option if symptoms continue. For now, we’re focusing on getting you stable at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What meds will I go home on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue metoclopramide, Zofran, and Compazine as needed for nausea. Pantoprazole daily, and your lisinopril, metoprolol, and citalopram.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, back to your usual 28 units of Lantus at night, plus Humalog as needed. We’ll review your sliding scale before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the lorazepam? It helped last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re prescribing two tablets at bedtime as needed for nausea. It can help with anxiety and vomiting, but use it sparingly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll be careful with it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re being discharged today. You’ve kept food down, your vitals are stable, and labs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. Thank you so much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep taking your meds, follow up with your GI doctor, and call if vomiting returns or you can’t keep fluids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ll also restart my blood pressure meds every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And monitor your blood sugar closely. We’re sending instructions home with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have your husband bring the car around. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my urine test came back with bacteria. Is that an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. It showed mixed flora, but that’s likely contamination from skin or genital area. No signs of infection, so no antibiotics needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No need. Just make sure to clean well before future samples if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, your anemia—we saw your hematocrit was 36, which is actually higher than usual for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought I was anemic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have a history of iron deficiency, but this time you were dehydrated, so your blood was concentrated. Your levels stayed stable, so no blood loss concern.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ll drink more fluids at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent plan. That’ll help everything—your blood pressure, kidneys, and digestion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take good care of myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best thing you can do. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You were admitted for vomiting again—can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been vomiting nonstop since yesterday—maybe 10 times. I just can’t keep anything down. I was only home a few days from the last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And it’s bilious—greenish? Any blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Green, yes. No blood that I’ve seen this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve reviewed your history—Type 1 diabetes, gastroparesis, gastric pacer, and you’ve had Botox in the stomach before. But your symptoms keep coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and the pacer didn’t help much. I thought maybe the Botox would, but it only lasted a little while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—for now. You’ll get fluids and medications through your port to help with nausea and hydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? It’s hard not eating. But I guess it’s necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, just until we get the vomiting under control. We also need to adjust your insulin since you’re not eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My sugars have been high. I’m worried about that too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your glucose was 273 when you came in—elevated, but not dangerous. We’ll give you a sliding scale and adjust your long-acting insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. My blood pressure’s been high too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was 190/100. We’ve increased your lisinopril and switched your metoprolol to the long-acting version. We may need IV meds if it stays high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on those for years. I don’t want a stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring closely. Your labs look stable—hemoglobin is 12, so no anemia right now. White count is slightly high, but no infection signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been so anxious lately. Is that part of this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Anxiety can definitely play a role. We’ve consulted GI and social work. There’s some discussion about whether this is more cyclic vomiting syndrome than gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s the difference?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Gastroparesis is delayed stomach emptying. Cyclic vomiting is more like migraine-related episodes—sudden, severe vomiting without a structural cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t get headaches though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not everyone does. Some people have it without migraines. We’re considering switching your antidepressant to amitriptyline—it can help prevent these episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on citalopram now. Is that okay to stop?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll taper it slowly—half a tablet daily for a week, then stop. Amitriptyline at bedtime may help with both mood and vomiting prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You didn’t vomit overnight—that’s great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I feel like I might still throw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: But you haven’t. We’d like to try a small amount of clear liquids today—if you tolerate that, we can advance your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can try. Just water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, small sips. We’ll monitor you closely. Your blood pressure is better—145/88 this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well—tolerating liquids, no vomiting. We’re going to try a soft diet today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have toast or applesauce?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Small portions. And we’ll keep your anti-nausea meds on board.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on Reglan for years. Is that still okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping it for now, but your GI doctor is concerned about long-term use—possible tardive dyskinesia. We’ll discuss alternatives at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve heard about that. Maybe we should stop it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor. For now, it’s helping. Also, your urine culture showed contamination—no infection, so no antibiotics needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, good. I was worried about a UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two full meals and no vomiting. That’s excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel almost normal. Can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. But there’s an option to stay one more night for an EGD with possible Botox repeat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to stay. I feel fine now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay. We’ll discharge you. But please call Dr. Patel’s office on Monday to schedule the EGD if you change your mind.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take amitriptyline at night, higher dose of lisinopril, and stay on Protonix. Zofran as needed, and Reglan before meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Resume your usual glargine dose at bedtime. Check sugars regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I need to see my psychiatrist too, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please follow up with them about the cyclic vomiting and anxiety. And your PCP for overall management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. You’ve been asymptomatic, eating well, and your vitals are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll call Dr. Patel and my psychiatrist this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. If vomiting returns, come back right away. Otherwise, we’ll see how the new meds work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope this time is different.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adjusting the plan to target cyclic vomiting more directly. Amitriptyline may make a difference. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during this hospital stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been vomiting since 5 a.m. I haven’t eaten anything, and it’s just watery. I also have a headache and felt chills earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve had episodes like this before, right? Does this feel similar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly like before. It’s the same pattern—nausea, then vomiting, and I just can’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. The nurses mentioned you sometimes make yourself vomit because it helps you feel better. Is that true?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… when I drink water or ginger ale, I feel worse unless I bring it up. It gives me some relief, even if it’s not normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But repeatedly inducing vomiting can cause serious problems—like electrolyte imbalances, damage to your esophagus, or even heart issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t realize it was that dangerous. I just do it because it feels like the only thing that helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll work on safer ways to manage that urge. For now, we’re going to keep you on IV fluids and give you medications to help with nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. My blood sugar’s probably high too, since I haven’t eaten but I’m still vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your glucose was 395 when you arrived. We’ve given you insulin and fluids to help correct that. We’ll keep monitoring it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My blood pressure’s always high during these episodes too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s 158/86 now, and your heart rate is elevated. That’s likely from the stress, vomiting, and maybe not absorbing your blood pressure meds because you’re vomiting them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I take metoprolol and lisinopril at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart those once you can keep oral meds down. For now, we may need to give you IV blood pressure medication if it stays high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been doing this for years—doctors always say it’s my diabetes or gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You do have type 1 diabetes and a history of gastroparesis, but your recent gastric motility study was normal. That makes us think this might not be purely a stomach-emptying issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what is it then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re considering that anxiety or a functional disorder might be playing a big role. The fact that you feel better after inducing vomiting suggests a behavioral component.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do get really anxious during these episodes. But it’s hard to tell what comes first—the nausea or the anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. They can feed into each other. We’re going to start you on Ativan for anxiety, which may also help with nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve never taken that before. Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s commonly used for anxiety and nausea. We’ll start low and only use it as needed. We’re also increasing your citalopram dose to 20 mg daily to help with mood and anxiety long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. I just want to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. I haven’t vomited since last night, and I didn’t make myself do it either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. Your labs are improving—your white count was high yesterday at 12.3, but it’s down to 9.8 this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. High white counts can happen with stress, vomiting, or dehydration. It’s coming down now that you’re more stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, good. My throat’s been a little sore too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning an EGD tomorrow to look into your stomach. We may do another botox injection, which has helped you before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I want to do that. It helped last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, we’ll take biopsies during the EGD to check for inflammation or infection, especially since your throat is sore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Sometimes people with diabetes get esophageal candidiasis. We’ll start fluconazole just in case, even before the biopsy results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I’ll take it as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from your EGD. The procedure went well. You received botox in the stomach, which may help reduce vomiting episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Did they see anything unusual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The endoscopist saw areas that looked like candidiasis, so biopsies were taken. But preliminary report says no fungal infection was found.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why do I have a sore throat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your glucose is now 275, and your anion gap is down to 17. That’s a big improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Morning… Is the vomiting from my diabetes or my stomach not emptying?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely both. Your gastroparesis means your stomach empties slowly, and when your sugars are high, it gets worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the anxiety? I know it makes it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, anxiety can trigger or worsen nausea. Psychiatry reviewed your case and recommended switching from Ativan to Klonopin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why the change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Klonopin may help with both anxiety and nausea long-term and has a lower risk of dependence. We’ll start it today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try it. I haven’t been great about seeing my psychiatrist, I know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay. The important thing is you’re here now. We’ll help you set up follow-up before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well overnight. You kept down a popsicle yesterday, and your nausea seems better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I haven’t vomited since last night. That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re going to try advancing your diet to clear liquids today, then maybe soft foods tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat regular food soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll take it step by step. If you tolerate the liquids, we’ll move forward. Your blood sugar needs to stay stable too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My sugars have been all over the place. I took my usual Lantus dose at home, but it didn’t help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common during flares. We gave you extra Humalog—35 units so far—and your sugars are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need to adjust my insulin at home too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll continue your sliding scale with Humalog. We’ll make sure you have clear instructions before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs look good. Glucose is 130, and your electrolytes are balanced. The alkalosis has resolved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my blood pressure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s still a bit high when you’re nauseous, but we switched you to captopril for now. You’ll go back to lisinopril at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m glad things are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. You’re eating a regular diet now and haven’t vomited in over 24 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better. Can I go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning to discharge you today. You’ll stop Ativan and start Klonopin twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I need to see a psychiatrist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, within a month, to continue the Klonopin. We also recommend following up with your diabetes team and PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t have a PCP right now… I was let go from my clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. We’ll help you find a new provider. Your health is important, and we want to support you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I really want to do better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We believe in you. Keep taking your medications, eat small meals, and reach out if nausea returns early.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And if I feel anxious, I should take the Klonopin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s meant to help prevent the cycle of anxiety and vomiting. Don’t wait until you’re very sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll have your discharge papers ready soon, and a nurse will go over your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready to go home and take care of myself better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You came in today because of nausea and vomiting, is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. It started this morning. I couldn’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve had this before, hasn’t it? It says here this is your tenth admission this year for similar symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it’s been really hard. It feels just like the last few times—sudden nausea, then vomiting, and I can’t eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on several medications for your gastroparesis and diabetes. Are you taking them as prescribed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking everything except the Lisinopril. My blood pressure felt low, so I stopped it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that might explain some of the high blood pressure we’re seeing now. But your nausea is likely tied to your gastroparesis flaring up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why my lactate was high in the ER?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Your lactate was 6.5, which is high, but it’s likely due to dehydration from vomiting. After fluids, it dropped to 1.5, which is much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not something more serious, like an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your blood cultures, and there’s no sign of infection so far. The high lactate was most likely from dehydration, not sepsis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My blood sugar was 238 earlier—should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s elevated, but not dangerously so. We’re giving you your usual insulin—Lantus at night and Humalog as needed. We switched from Levemir to Lantus temporarily since we don’t carry Levemir here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I’ll go back to Levemir at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. We’re just using Lantus for now at a lower dose to be safe. You didn’t have any low sugars, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my nausea? The meds in the ER didn’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you IV fluids and a combination of anti-nausea meds—Zofran, Reglan, Ativan, and Compazine. We’ll keep monitoring how you respond.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on Reglan and Amitriptyline at home. Should we increase the Amitriptyline like GI suggested before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, we’re keeping your Amitriptyline at 10mg. GI had suggested increasing it, but we’ll discuss that with them again before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my blood pressure is still high—should we treat it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re right, it’s elevated—222 over 100 when you arrived. But since you’re not having headaches or chest pain, and this often happens with nausea, we’re focusing on treating the nausea first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So once the nausea improves, my pressure should come down?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the plan. We’ve restarted your Lisinopril today, and as you rehydrate and the vomiting stops, your pressure should stabilize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re looking better. Your nausea has improved, and you kept down some ice chips. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better, actually. I haven’t vomited since last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your labs also look better. Your bicarbonate is up to 27, so the acidosis has resolved. Your lactate is normal now too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the acidosis was from vomiting and dehydration?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. When you lose fluids from vomiting, your body can become acidic. The fluids and stopping the vomiting helped correct that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my blood count? My hemoglobin was low at 9.2.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a bit low, but it’s consistent with your previous levels. When you were dehydrated, your hematocrit was falsely high at 36. Now that you’re rehydrated, it’s down to 28.7, which matches your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s stable. You still have mild anemia, likely from iron deficiency, and you’re scheduled for a colonoscopy soon to check for sources of blood loss.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. And my blood pressure is down to 140/85 now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. It’s responding well to the Lisinopril and treating the nausea. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to advance your diet today. You’ve tolerated ice chips and clear liquids. We’ll try full liquids next.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you keep tolerating food and your nausea stays under control, yes. We’ll aim for discharge tomorrow afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well overnight—no vomiting, and you ate a full liquid breakfast. We’re going to discharge you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Are my meds the same as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re sending you home with your usual medications: Lisinopril, citalopram, clonazepam, amitriptyline, pantoprazole, and metoclopramide. And resume your Levemir and Humalog as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No changes at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No changes. We didn’t increase the amitriptyline this time, but we recommend you follow up with GI and psychiatry to discuss long-term management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I need to see them. It’s just hard to keep up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But staying on top of your meds and follow-ups can help prevent these frequent admissions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. Thank you for helping me through this again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and call your doctor if the nausea comes back or if you can’t keep fluids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during this stay. You were just admitted for nausea and vomiting again, is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I just can’t keep anything down. I feel so sick every time I try to eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your blood pressure was very high when you came in—194 over 94. That’s concerning. Did you notice any headaches or chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no chest pain or headaches. Just the nausea and throwing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. We’re giving you IV fluids to help with dehydration. Your lab work showed a high lactate level earlier—4.6—which suggests your body was under stress from not having enough fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Lactate? Is that like acidosis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s called lactic acidosis. But after three liters of IV fluids, your lactate dropped to 1.0, which is normal. So that’s improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s good. But why does this keep happening? I was just here two days ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we’re trying to understand. You have gastroparesis, which means your stomach empties slowly. But we’ve also noticed that sometimes vomiting happens right after you drink or eat, even if it’s small amounts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t help it. I just feel so full and sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But one of the nurses saw you induce vomiting after drinking water. Is that something you do when you feel anxious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I… I don’t know. Maybe. It just feels like the only way to stop the nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I want you to know we’re not judging you. But induced vomiting can make everything worse—dehydration, acidosis, even high blood pressure. It’s a cycle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So you think it’s in my head?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not exactly. Your gastroparesis is real. But the way you respond—vomiting right after intake—suggests a behavioral pattern, possibly linked to anxiety. That’s why psychiatry has been consulted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve missed some appointments. I know I should go, but I get too anxious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay. The important thing is recognizing it now. We can help you set up a new appointment before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still nauseous, but I didn’t vomit last night. I tried sipping water slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. Your blood pressure is better too—142 over 88 this morning. We’ve switched you from IV labetalol to oral meds: lisinopril and amlodipine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on lisinopril before. Why the new one?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because your blood pressure was so high, we needed an extra medication. Amlodipine helps relax your blood vessels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my insulin? My sugars have been high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you glargine at night and lispro with meals. Since you’re not eating much, we’re using a sliding scale to adjust doses safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had the gastric pacer for a reason. Why isn’t it helping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pacer helps some, but it can’t override the effects of frequent vomiting or anxiety. We also discussed a J-tube, but you decided against it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want surgery. I just want to stop feeling like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And that’s possible. But it will take work—both medically and with mental health support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray yesterday was clear—no pneumonia or aspiration. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was worried about that. I’ve thrown up so much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. But your lungs look good. The main issue remains the cycle of vomiting, dehydration, and high blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been thinking. Maybe the vomiting does help me feel temporary relief, but then I feel worse after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a really important insight. It’s like a coping mechanism, but it’s harming your body in the long run.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what can I do instead?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll work with psychiatry to find strategies—maybe different medications or therapy techniques to manage the urge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve gone two full days without vomiting. That’s a big improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel nauseous, but I’ve been using the Zofran and trying deep breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. And your labs are stable—no acidosis, hemoglobin is holding, and your electrolytes are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow, yes. But we want to make sure you’re safe with follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll go to psychiatry this time. I promise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll schedule it before you leave. And we’re giving you Zofran for breakthrough nausea, plus your regular Reglan and Nexium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take lisinopril 10 mg three times a day and amlodipine twice daily. We lowered the lisinopril dose to avoid low BP now that you’re hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check before discharge. You’ve been off IV fluids for 24 hours, eating small meals, and no vomiting. How do you feel?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tired, but better. I’m scared it’ll come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. But you’ve made real progress by acknowledging the role of anxiety. That’s the first step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep working on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll support you. Discharge is set for tomorrow morning. Rest up, and the nurse will review your meds and instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Remember: take your meds, eat small meals, and call if nausea returns. Most importantly—keep your psychiatry appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really want to get better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And we believe you can. Take care.

conversation_lines.text: Still nauseous, honestly. I’ve been trying not to throw up, but it’s hard. I’ve been so stressed lately—getting ready to start the insulin pump. I think that’s making everything worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Stress can definitely trigger your gastroparesis and affect your blood sugar. We’ve started you on IV fluids and insulin to correct the DKA. Your anion gap was high at 24, but it’s already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the DKA is getting better? I was scared when they said that in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s resolving. Your latest labs show your bicarbonate is up to 24 and your anion gap is now 19—much better. We’ll keep the IV insulin running for a bit longer, then switch back to your usual injections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. But the nausea… it’s still there. I took Zofran at home, but it didn’t help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve added several anti-nausea meds: IV Zofran, Compazine, and we’re continuing your home Reglan. We also gave you Ativan in the ER, which helps with both nausea and anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do take Ativan at home, but clonazepam usually works better for me. Can I take that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re avoiding clonazepam this admission. We’ll use lorazepam instead, which is similar, and it’s on your discharge plan. We want to keep things consistent with what’s safest for you long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I guess that’s fine. I just want to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re working on it. Your heart rate is still high—around 115. That’s common with dehydration and DKA, but it’s been persistent in past admissions too. We’ve checked for thyroid issues and infections before, and nothing’s shown up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it’s always high when I’m in the hospital. I think it’s from the anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s very possible. Your EKG shows sinus tachycardia, which fits. No signs of heart strain. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I just reviewed your overnight labs. Your glucose is down to 231, and your kidney function is improving—creatinine is now 0.7. You’re definitely on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I haven’t thrown up since last night. I think I’m starting to feel a little better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’re going to try advancing your diet to clear liquids later today, if you’re up for it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. But sometimes even water makes me feel worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go slow. And we’ll keep the IV fluids running for now. Your team also noted that in past admissions, there were times when vomiting was self-induced. Is that something you’ve thought about?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I… I do sometimes make myself throw up when the nausea gets overwhelming. But only when I feel like I have to. It’s not that I’m faking it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I believe you. This pattern—severe nausea, vomiting, frequent admissions—has been seen in conditions like rumination syndrome or cyclic vomiting, which can be linked to anxiety. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My husband and I talked about it. We both think the stress of the pump transition is setting it off again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a really important insight. Managing stress could help prevent future episodes. We’d like to connect you with a psychologist you trust. Would you be open to that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to see the hospital psychiatrist, but I can find someone in my town. I just need to feel in control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely fair. We’ll support whatever therapist you choose. The goal is to help you manage these episodes before they lead to another hospital stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You slept well, I hear. You had a soft diet last night and kept it down. That’s a big step forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had applesauce and toast. Felt okay. Nausea is much better today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Your labs this morning are stable. No ketones, normal electrolytes. We’re going to stop the IV fluids and switch your insulin back to your home regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m going home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We want to make sure you’re consistently tolerating food and that your blood sugar stays in range. We’ll check again tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I really don’t want to be readmitted again. It’s exhausting.

conversation_lines.text: And we want to help you avoid that. That’s why managing stress and having a mental health plan is so important. You’ve already made progress by recognizing the pattern.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’m feeling more like myself. I haven’t taken any extra Ativan today, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a sign your anxiety is better controlled. We’ll send you home with ondansetron and lorazepam for breakthrough nausea, but the goal is to use them sparingly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my clonazepam? I usually take it twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: Good news. Your labs are stable, you’ve tolerated a soft diet, and you haven’t vomited in over 24 hours. We’re clearing you for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.text: Continue all your home meds except clonazepam. Take the new ondansetron and lorazepam only if nausea returns. Follow up with your endocrinologist, and please make that therapist appointment. Stress management is key.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve already thought about who I want to see. I don’t want this to keep happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best step you can take. You’re strong, and you’re not alone in this. We’re here to support you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have your husband come up when you’re ready. Get some rest and take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call if anything changes—especially blood sugar or nausea that won’t go away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve learned my limits.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s half the battle. Keep listening to your body.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m going to take it one day at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best way. You’ve done really well this admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I feel like I understand my body better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s huge. Knowledge is power, especially with chronic conditions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m going to start that journal I’ve been putting off—track my stress, food, blood sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s an excellent idea. It could help you and your doctors see patterns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to take control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you’re on your way. We’re proud of you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve earned it. Now go home and rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Take care, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having really bad nausea and vomiting since early this morning. It feels just like my old gastroparesis episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any abdominal pain, fever, or diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no pain or fever. Just the nausea and vomiting. I couldn’t keep anything down, not even water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also see you have type 1 diabetes. How has your blood sugar been?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The night before, it dropped to 38. I ate peanut butter and crackers, but it only went up to 60. I turned off my insulin pump because I was scared of going low again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll monitor your glucose closely. For now, we’re going to keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—for a few hours to let your stomach settle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but I’m really worried about my blood sugar going high if I’m not eating and not on the pump.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a valid concern. We’ll give you IV insulin to keep your levels in check. An endocrine specialist will help manage that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I also took lorazepam at home, and it helped a little with the nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve given you ondansetron and more lorazepam. We’ll continue those as needed. We also started a proton-pump inhibitor in case there’s any irritation from vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs came back. Your sodium is a bit low at 130, likely from vomiting and not drinking. We’re giving you IV fluids to correct that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s mild and we’re treating it. You should be fine with the fluids. Your kidney function is okay, so it should correct quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed a small amount of coffee-ground material in your vomit earlier. Did you see that too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t notice, but I was pretty out of it. Is that blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly a small amount, likely from irritation due to retching. Your hemoglobin is stable, so no active bleeding. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I was dry heaving a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your white blood cell count was high last night—15.9—but it’s already coming down. We did a chest X-ray to check for infection, and it’s clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it an infection then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unlikely. No fever, clean urine, and normal lungs. It’s probably a stress response from the vomiting and high glucose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. That’s good to hear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar was up to 395 this morning with an anion gap of 21. That means you had mild ketoacidosis. But it’s already improving with insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought stopping the pump would prevent highs, but I guess not eating made it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Without insulin, even without food, your body makes glucose. We’re glad the gap is closing quickly. No signs of infection or other triggers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it’s under control now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures came back with no growth so far. That’s reassuring—no bloodstream infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. And my nausea is definitely better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your vitals are stabilizing. Heart rate is down from 103 to 88. Your blood pressure was a bit high earlier, so we restarted your lisinopril.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forgot to ask—was my Port-A-Cath checked? I know it’s there, but I wanted to make sure it’s okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the chest X-ray confirmed it’s in place and unchanged. No complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel a lot safer knowing that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news. You’ve gone over 24 hours without vomiting. We’re going to start you on clear liquids and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Can I have some broth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with broth and water. If you tolerate it, we’ll advance to soft foods later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well with the liquids. How’s your stomach feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. No nausea at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’re going to switch you to a soft diet—mashed potatoes, applesauce, things like that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your sodium is now 133, and your glucose is 182. Both are much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I go back on my insulin pump?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to restart it tomorrow morning. The endocrine team approved it since your levels are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m really relieved. I feel like I’m getting back to normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You tolerated a regular diet last night with no issues. We’ve restarted your insulin pump with a basal rate of 0.75 units per hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My blood sugar this morning was 261—should I be concerned?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a bit high, but not alarming. It’ll settle as you resume normal eating. Just keep checking your fingersticks as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back on lisinopril, amitriptyline, and clonazepam. We’re adding ondansetron for nausea as needed, and docusate and senna for constipation prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take those as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’re planning to discharge you today. Your vitals are stable, and you’re tolerating food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you leave, let’s go over your discharge instructions. Your nausea was due to gastroparesis, and we managed it with medications and diet advancement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the high blood sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was from holding your insulin when you were NPO. Going forward, even if you’re not eating, you still need some insulin. We’ll adjust the pump settings if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll be more careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, keep taking the new meds—ondansetron for nausea, and the stool softeners. Follow up with your primary doctor in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re discharging you home in good condition. Call us if you start vomiting again or if your blood sugar goes out of range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your husband is here, right? He can help you get settled at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, he’s waiting outside. He’s been so supportive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Make sure to rest and take it easy for the next few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave—any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m all set. Everything’s clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Have a safe trip home.
